extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction (authors studying characterization and narrative craft)
extracted.subtask_description: Illustrative criteria and norms for crafting characters, social critique, and narrative choices in realist/early-20th-century literary fiction; useful for authors analyzing characterization, moral stance, and how topical subject-matter affects reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness versus mere contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers declared contentment to be happiness, arguing that the hod-carrier was likely to be happier in his hut than the millionaire in his palace; but was not that mere animal contentment...the ignorance of one whose eyes have never been raised to the heights?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valorizes a conception of happiness that goes beyond material sufficiency: true happiness includes higher intellectual, aesthetic, or spiritual aspirations. Use contrast (e.g., common contentment vs. awareness of higher states) to evaluate a character's inner life and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity/independence over inherited wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson loved money for what pleasure it could give but would never allow money to dominate his life; he declined his father's lucrative offers and resolved to earn his own living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray protagonists who refuse easy, compromised prosperity in order to preserve moral agency and self-respect. Depict concrete actions (refusing positions, refusing settlements) to signal integrity rather than merely asserting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth's burdens and moral cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The lot of the world's richest man was far from enviable—baited by yellow newspapers, investigated, dogged by process-servers, haunted by beggars, harassed by blackmailers...the galley slave led a life of luxurious ease compared with John Burkett Ryder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating wealthy characters, include the social, legal, and moral consequences of riches (scrutiny, hostility, isolation) to avoid glamorizing wealth; use those costs as thematic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic vocation requires persistence and self-education
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson had dreamed of a literary or art career; after initial rebuffs he refused to be discouraged, kept on, and eventually succeeded—academy training, illustrating for magazines, then commissions leading to a studio and income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray artistic success as earned through study, apprenticeship, persistence after rejection, and gradual recognition; include concrete milestones (training, first acceptances, notable commissions) to make the trajectory believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary success can depend on subject and timeliness as much as skill
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the subject rather than the skill of the narrator that counted in the book's success...the book had come out at a timely moment, when the whole world was talking of the Money Peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that topicality, controversy, and timing influence reception; authors or reviewers should weigh subject choice and social moment alongside craft when assessing a work's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pseudonym/anonymity to protect author and family
rubrics_metrics.description: The book had been published under the pseudonym 'Shirley Green'...she was careful her identity should remain a secret (as daughter of a Supreme Court judge she would not embarrass her father).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fiction closely parallels living figures or sensitive subjects, consider anonymity or pseudonyms as a narrative/strategic choice; depict the motives, risks, and measures (anonymous mailing, secrecy) to make that choice plausible in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: depth ('soul and character') over mere aesthetic beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty is only skin deep...The merely beautiful woman...presents absolutely no key to the soul within...Shirley was not beautiful, but hers was a face that never failed to attract attention. It was a thoughtful and interesting face...there was in her face something far more appealing--soul and character."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value markers of inner life—expression, thoughtfulness, will—over flawless physical features. Use specific, slightly irregular features and expressive details (brow, mouth, eyes) to signal psychological complexity and moral strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male desirability: refinement, strength of character, and personal courage
rubrics_metrics.description: "She demanded in a man the refinement of the true gentleman, together with strength of character and personal courage." Jefferson is described as manly, frank, cordial, with a fighting jaw and steel-blue eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing romantic interests or heroes in this social register, foreground comportment (gentlemanly manners), moral fiber (strength of character), and visible courage. Combine social refinement with physical and moral traits to create an admirable male figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female professional ambition vs matrimony
rubrics_metrics.description: She had made up her mind that she would never marry. ...she was fascinated by her literary work and she was practical enough to know that matrimony, with its visions of slippers and cradles, would be fatal to any ambition of that kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a credible tension between domestic expectations and artistic ambition: outline the practical obstacles marriage poses to a woman's career, and let the character's choices reflect deliberate prioritization rather than mere romanticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity versus poseur affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Like most of the men you see there are from the provinces...they are notorious poseurs, aping the dress and manners of the old-time student...Nobody took them seriously except themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between characters who are genuinely committed to a pursuit and those who merely adopt its trappings. Use description of habits, consistency of behavior (e.g., attending lectures, reading) and consequences (ruined by excess vs matured by experience) to mark authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social refinement signalled by cleanliness, taste, and distinct social spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Shirley believed in an aristocracy of brains and soap...no clean person...should be expected to sit close in public places to persons who were not on speaking terms with the bath-tub...The French lower classes knew their place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a narrator endorses social hierarchy, use details of dress, public behaviour, hygiene, and segregated spaces to show how characters perceive and enact refinement; such portrayals also reveal narrator bias and social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical composed behavior in confrontation (know the law/rates and keep decorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shirley lays down the law to the cocher about the tariff, calmly stating times and rates and offering to continue argument at a police-station if necessary; Jefferson wants 'no scandal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict effective, composed confrontation by having characters assert factual knowledge and offer controlled consequences rather than resorting to theatrics; contrasts between a calm, informed actor and an impulsive protector can reveal character dynamics.
